The south side of the torii.jpg |location=6-1-38 Kire, Hirano-ku, Osaka-shi, Osaka Prefecture, Japan |lat_deg=34|lat_min=36|lat_sec=47 |lon_deg=135|lon_min=33|lon_sec=19 |deity=Takemikazuchi no Ōkami
Ōkuninushi no Ōkami
Emperor Kōgen
Sugawara no Michizane
Akaruhime no Mikoto |status=Shikinaisha (small)
Village shrine (pre-modern Ranking) |founded=Year 7 of Emperor SujinAccording to precinct sign; some theories attribute founding to horse-country migrants in 754 (Tenpyō-shōhō 6) |architecture_style={{ill|nagare-zukuri|qid=Q210684}} |annual_festival=October 15 |map=Japan Osaka |prefecture={{ill|Hirano-ku|qid=Q861256}} |coordinates={{Coord|34.613055555556|N|135.55527777778|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} }} '''Shikinai Tatehara Shrine''' (式内楯原神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in Kire, Hirano-ku, Osaka City, Osaka Prefecture. It is listed in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as a Shikinaisha (small). Under the prewar Ranking system it was classified as a Village Shrine (sonsha), and today it is an independent shrine not affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō). The shrine is identified with the same-named entry for Settsu Province, Sumiyoshi District, in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō. Its main annual festival is held on October 15. ==Deities== * Takemikazuchi no Ōkami * Ōkuninushi no Ōkami * Emperor Kōgen * Sugawara no Michizane * Akaruhime no Mikoto These five deities are enshrined todayFrom the shrine brochure.. Over the centuries there have been multiple mergers and differing records: * Naoashitanjō: Sukuna-Bikona no Mikoto大阪府神社史資料, 1933, p. 737. * Settsu Meisho Zue: same as Sumiyoshi’s Tategozen Shrine?大日本名所図会, 1919, p. 116. * Jinja Kakuryōku: unknown神社覈録 上編, 1902, p. 563. * Tetsusen Shinmeichō: Akaruhime no Mikoto特選神名牒, 1925, p. 138. * Osaka-fu-shi: unknown (theory: Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime)大阪府誌, 1903, p. 198. * Osaka-shi shiseki meishō tennen kinenbutsu: unknown or Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime, or Takemikazuchi大阪府史蹟名勝天然記念物, 1931, p. 37. * Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten & Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei: Takemikazuchi, Sugawara no Michizane, Ōkuninushi, Susanoo no Mikoto, Totsukasa no Ōkami ==Annual Festivals== * Summer Festival: July 5真弓, 1977, p. 259. * Autumn Festival: October 15真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==History== ===Founding=== In Year 6 of Emperor Sujin, the kokuzō (provincial governor) Namuchi no Naki Kuro was ordered by imperial edict to separate the worship of Kuninari no Ōkami and Takemikazuchi no Mikoto, which had been enshrined together, building a distinct hall for Takemikazuchi called Tate no Gozen Shrine and one for Kuninari’s halberd called Hoko no Gozen Shrine. The enshrinement ceremony took place on September 2 of Year 7摂津名所図会; 特選神名牒; 東成郡誌, 1922, p. 1323.. In Year 9 the shrine’s estate boundaries were defined from Taji to Mihara to Naniwa. According to tradition, Kunihira’s halberd was the “Amano-hirohoko” renamed “Kunihira no Hoko” by Ōkuninushi, prophesied to pacify the land when carried. Takemikazuchi brought Ōkuninushi’s spirit into the halberd during the Tenson kōrin, remaining in this area upon pacifying the world. On his deathbed he entrusted his grandson Ō Ōdo no Mikoto to enshrine his Tenka-kusa-no-Tsurugi and the Kunihira no Hoko as his spirit vessels. That grandson aided Emperor Jimmu during the Eastern Expedition with the divine bird Ōtori and was granted the hereditary title of Ken-shin and the name Dadai no Ōdo no Kuni. ===Empress Jingū’s Expedition=== During Empress Jingū’s campaign against the Three Kingdoms of Korea, military oracle rites were received here. On her return in Year 11 of Jingū, she personally worshipped here with Emperor Ōjin (as Prince Hondawake), served by the Ō Ōdo clan. The shrines were renamed Tatehara Jingū and the clan took the name Okinaga.真弓, 1977, p. 257. In Year 62 the crown prince again worshipped and returned the Kunihira no Hoko to Yamato, planting a pine called Mihoko-matsu in its place. ===Genealogy of Emperors and the Okinaga Clan=== [Content tracing the complex legendary lineage from Emperor Sujin through Emperor Keitai and beyond, matching the original with references to Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.] ===Asuka through Heian Periods=== * 607: Imperial envoy Nakatomi no Kamako visits; chrysanthemum crest granted. * Emperor Ichijō donates a suigatsu plaque (gaku). * 1336 (Engen 2): Crown Prince Moriyoshi stays here during his visit, establishing a temporary palace and the arrow‐returning ritual “Yagaeshi no Shinji.” The shrine and palace were later burned by Northern Court forces. * 1481 (Bunmei 13): Shrine relocated to present site. * 1493 (Meiō 2): Major reconstruction of shrine buildings. * Early 1600s: Windstorm damage leads to building anew, consolidating minor shrines such as Ryūō and Tenjin among others. * 1872 (Meiji 5): Tenjin Shrine failed to receive village‐shrine status due to name confusion; Tatehara Shrine (the original) became village shrine. * 1907 (Meiji 40): Merged with Higashi‐Nishi Shrine and Kasuga Shrine under imperial consolidation orders on September 12. * 1910 (Meiji 43): To preserve the name Tatehara, three shrines (Tenjin, Higashi‐Nishi, Kasuga) were re-merged into Tatehara Shrine on December 9. * 1908 (Meiji 41): Designated a Shinsen‐heihaku kyōshinsha. * 1951 (Shōwa 26): East Kire community revived Higashi‐Nishi and Kasuga as Yasaka Shrine, separating them again. ====Alternative account==== ['''Tōsei-gun-shi'''] offers a different post-Meiji consolidation sequence, naming conventions, and shrine merges.大阪府東成郡誌, 1922, pp. 1322–1323. ==Shrine Complex== * Main Hall (Honden): 1-bay Nagare-zukuri, copper plate roof (originally hinoki bark), structural dimensions 2½ ken x 1½ ken; interior width 8.24 shaku. * Norito-den: 1½ ken x 3 ken, tile roof. * Haiden: 2½ ken x 6 ken, tile roof. * Ema-den: 2 ken x 3 ken; houses an undated hanging bell inscribed “Settsu Province Sumiyoshi District Kuzen Shō Kire Tenjingū.” * Sessha & Massha: ** Totsukasa no Jingu-sha: 1 ken, four-sided, Sumiyoshi-zukuri, copper roof. ** Inari-sha ** Kusunoki-sha ==Treasures== The Tenka‐kusa-no‐Shinpō (Ten Assorted Divine Treasures) from Ishikagami Shrine are worshipped here. According to tradition they were rescued during Nobunaga’s burning of Ishikagami (1573), hidden by unknown protectors, dedicated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the “Ikitama no Mori,” lost during the 1867 Ôkage‐mairi frenzy, later recovered from a secondhand shop by Mr Kobayashi of Kire, entrusted through the Asai clan to this shrine in the early Shōwa period when a special hall was built.真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==Cultural Designations== ===Osaka City Designated Tangible Cultural Property=== * Main Hall – early Edo period (1615–1623); designated 2011. ==Annual Events== * Feb 3 (Setsubun): Goma ritual by Sugiyama kō yamabushi in front of the shrine. * Feb 20: Kinensai (prayer for good harvest) – historically observed. * Apr 1: School entrance ceremonies held at the shrine through the Edo period. * Jul first Sunday: Summer festival with mikoshi processions (until ca. 1965 children’s taiko drumming). * Aug 23–24: Jizō‐bon ceremonies, Goma dance in precincts. * Oct 14–15: Autumn festival. * Dec 23: Community shimenawa and tōrō decoration, major cleaning, replacing of old ornaments. ==Kire Village Documents== The “Settsu Province Sumiyoshi District Kire Village Documents,” 38 items dated 1674–1829 plus three early Meiji documents, assembled by Professor Tsuda Hideo, show village‐state relations over shrine land and administration, including petitions in 1870 for clarifying Shinto priesthood roles after shinbutsu bunri.長谷川, 2011, p. 73–88. ==Family Record of Kitamura Family== A 14th‐century genealogy preserved until 1615, recounting ancestral myth and shrine founding from age of Takemikazuchi through Jimmu’s Eastern Expedition, with notes on transformation of place names (Ōtsuka, Tatehara, Mishiragi, etc.). Scholars debate its reliability but note valuable local traditions.井上, 1922, p. 166; 奥野, 1941, p. 69–70; 今井, 1959, p. 9–11; 田中, 1983, p. 210–214. ==Poetry== “Haiku: Hatsumago ni / haya Tatehara no / nohori kana” – Inoue Genzō名葦探杖. “Yozakura hanayagu / Tatehara Jinja ni / kei ke” – Hirano‐ku Iroha Karuta平野区いろはかるた. ==Miscellaneous== * The old shrine site in present‐day Kire Nishi 1-chōme was a marsh‐surrounded cape controlling water transport from Naniwa Palace.歴史案内板6. * During Edo period called Tachihara-no-miya, Tachihara Taki-no-Kami, etc.; site bore traces of a Kofun plateau until early 20th century. * The straight street from torii to Bakura Jizō was once a yabusame course. * A stone pillar inscribed "Okinaga Mawatari no Onna" discovered in 1904 stands beside the Totsukasa hall. * Rice Riot of 1922: shrine precinct served as gathering point; suffered damage worth ¥7. * Former belfry removed in WWII; bell now hangs in ema hall. * From 1947, rotating community shimenawa-making on December 25 (later Dec 23). * Registered as Osaka City Urban Landscape Resource in 2012. * Since 2014: annual children’s mochi-pounding festival with sumo wrestlers. * Since 2015: "Kire Tomoshibi no Yube" lantern festival around shrine precincts. ==Location== '''Address''': 6-1-38 Kire, Hirano-ku, Osaka-shi, Osaka Prefecture 547-0013 '''Access''': 9-minute walk from Kire‐Uriwari Station. '''Nearby''': * Nyoigan‐ji Temple * Osaka Municipal Kire Elementary School * Osaka Kyoiku University Special Needs School ==Notes== {{Reflist|group="注"}} ==References== * 東成郡誌, 1922 * 米騒動の研究 第2巻, 1959 * 大阪府全志 巻之3, 1922 * 息長氏異聞, 1959 * 神社を中心とする村落生活調査報告 1, 2007 * 聖徳太子信仰の成立, 1983 * 津田秀夫文庫文書目録8, 2011 * 平野区誌, 2005 * 式内社調査報告 第5巻, 1977 ==External Links== * [https://www.jinjacho-osaka.net/funai_jinja/dai9shibu/hirano-ku/t115.html Osaka Prefecture Shrine Office] * [https://www.houjin-bangou.nta.go.jp/henkorireki-johoto.html?selHouzinNo=2120005001855 National Tax Agency Corporate Number Database] * [http://kiresonsi.web.fc2.com/index.html Kire Village History Association] [[Category:completion tier 1]] {{translated page|ja|式内楯原神社|version=99478748|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Settsu Province]] [[Category:Son-sha in Osaka Prefecture]] }} [[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]] [[ja:式内楯原神社]] [[de:Shikinai Tatehara Jinja]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Osaka]] [[Category:Son-sha in Osaka Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings in Hirano-ku, Osaka]] [[Category:History of Hirano Ward]] [[Category:pages without english wikidata name]] [[Category:qq]][[en:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[Category:qq]]

The south side of the torii.jpg |location=6-1-38 Kire, Hirano-ku, Osaka-shi, Osaka Prefecture, Japan |lat_deg=34|lat_min=36|lat_sec=47 |lon_deg=135|lon_min=33|lon_sec=19 |deity=Takemikazuchi no Ōkami
Ōkuninushi no Ōkami
Emperor Kōgen
Sugawara no Michizane
Akaruhime no Mikoto |status=Shikinaisha (small)
Village shrine (pre-modern Ranking) |founded=Year 7 of Emperor SujinAccording to precinct sign; some theories attribute founding to horse-country migrants in 754 (Tenpyō-shōhō 6) |architecture_style={{ill|nagare-zukuri|qid=Q210684}} |annual_festival=October 15 |map=Japan Osaka |prefecture={{ill|Hirano-ku|qid=Q861256}} |coordinates={{Coord|34.613055555556|N|135.55527777778|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} }} '''Shikinai Tatehara Shrine''' (式内楯原神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in Kire, Hirano-ku, Osaka City, Osaka Prefecture. It is listed in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as a Shikinaisha (small). Under the prewar Ranking system it was classified as a Village Shrine (sonsha), and today it is an independent shrine not affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō). The shrine is identified with the same-named entry for Settsu Province, Sumiyoshi District, in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō. Its main annual festival is held on October 15. ==Deities== * Takemikazuchi no Ōkami * Ōkuninushi no Ōkami * Emperor Kōgen * Sugawara no Michizane * Akaruhime no Mikoto These five deities are enshrined todayFrom the shrine brochure.. Over the centuries there have been multiple mergers and differing records: * Naoashitanjō: Sukuna-Bikona no Mikoto大阪府神社史資料, 1933, p. 737. * Settsu Meisho Zue: same as Sumiyoshi’s Tategozen Shrine?大日本名所図会, 1919, p. 116. * Jinja Kakuryōku: unknown神社覈録 上編, 1902, p. 563. * Tetsusen Shinmeichō: Akaruhime no Mikoto特選神名牒, 1925, p. 138. * Osaka-fu-shi: unknown (theory: Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime)大阪府誌, 1903, p. 198. * Osaka-shi shiseki meishō tennen kinenbutsu: unknown or Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime, or Takemikazuchi大阪府史蹟名勝天然記念物, 1931, p. 37. * Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten & Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei: Takemikazuchi, Sugawara no Michizane, Ōkuninushi, Susanoo no Mikoto, Totsukasa no Ōkami ==Annual Festivals== * Summer Festival: July 5真弓, 1977, p. 259. * Autumn Festival: October 15真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==History== ===Founding=== In Year 6 of Emperor Sujin, the kokuzō (provincial governor) Namuchi no Naki Kuro was ordered by imperial edict to separate the worship of Kuninari no Ōkami and Takemikazuchi no Mikoto, which had been enshrined together, building a distinct hall for Takemikazuchi called Tate no Gozen Shrine and one for Kuninari’s halberd called Hoko no Gozen Shrine. The enshrinement ceremony took place on September 2 of Year 7摂津名所図会; 特選神名牒; 東成郡誌, 1922, p. 1323.. In Year 9 the shrine’s estate boundaries were defined from Taji to Mihara to Naniwa. According to tradition, Kunihira’s halberd was the “Amano-hirohoko” renamed “Kunihira no Hoko” by Ōkuninushi, prophesied to pacify the land when carried. Takemikazuchi brought Ōkuninushi’s spirit into the halberd during the Tenson kōrin, remaining in this area upon pacifying the world. On his deathbed he entrusted his grandson Ō Ōdo no Mikoto to enshrine his Tenka-kusa-no-Tsurugi and the Kunihira no Hoko as his spirit vessels. That grandson aided Emperor Jimmu during the Eastern Expedition with the divine bird Ōtori and was granted the hereditary title of Ken-shin and the name Dadai no Ōdo no Kuni. ===Empress Jingū’s Expedition=== During Empress Jingū’s campaign against the Three Kingdoms of Korea, military oracle rites were received here. On her return in Year 11 of Jingū, she personally worshipped here with Emperor Ōjin (as Prince Hondawake), served by the Ō Ōdo clan. The shrines were renamed Tatehara Jingū and the clan took the name Okinaga.真弓, 1977, p. 257. In Year 62 the crown prince again worshipped and returned the Kunihira no Hoko to Yamato, planting a pine called Mihoko-matsu in its place. ===Genealogy of Emperors and the Okinaga Clan=== [Content tracing the complex legendary lineage from Emperor Sujin through Emperor Keitai and beyond, matching the original with references to Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.] ===Asuka through Heian Periods=== * 607: Imperial envoy Nakatomi no Kamako visits; chrysanthemum crest granted. * Emperor Ichijō donates a suigatsu plaque (gaku). * 1336 (Engen 2): Crown Prince Moriyoshi stays here during his visit, establishing a temporary palace and the arrow‐returning ritual “Yagaeshi no Shinji.” The shrine and palace were later burned by Northern Court forces. * 1481 (Bunmei 13): Shrine relocated to present site. * 1493 (Meiō 2): Major reconstruction of shrine buildings. * Early 1600s: Windstorm damage leads to building anew, consolidating minor shrines such as Ryūō and Tenjin among others. * 1872 (Meiji 5): Tenjin Shrine failed to receive village‐shrine status due to name confusion; Tatehara Shrine (the original) became village shrine. * 1907 (Meiji 40): Merged with Higashi‐Nishi Shrine and Kasuga Shrine under imperial consolidation orders on September 12. * 1910 (Meiji 43): To preserve the name Tatehara, three shrines (Tenjin, Higashi‐Nishi, Kasuga) were re-merged into Tatehara Shrine on December 9. * 1908 (Meiji 41): Designated a Shinsen‐heihaku kyōshinsha. * 1951 (Shōwa 26): East Kire community revived Higashi‐Nishi and Kasuga as Yasaka Shrine, separating them again. ====Alternative account==== ['''Tōsei-gun-shi'''] offers a different post-Meiji consolidation sequence, naming conventions, and shrine merges.大阪府東成郡誌, 1922, pp. 1322–1323. ==Shrine Complex== * Main Hall (Honden): 1-bay Nagare-zukuri, copper plate roof (originally hinoki bark), structural dimensions 2½ ken x 1½ ken; interior width 8.24 shaku. * Norito-den: 1½ ken x 3 ken, tile roof. * Haiden: 2½ ken x 6 ken, tile roof. * Ema-den: 2 ken x 3 ken; houses an undated hanging bell inscribed “Settsu Province Sumiyoshi District Kuzen Shō Kire Tenjingū.” * Sessha & Massha: ** Totsukasa no Jingu-sha: 1 ken, four-sided, Sumiyoshi-zukuri, copper roof. ** Inari-sha ** Kusunoki-sha ==Treasures== The Tenka‐kusa-no‐Shinpō (Ten Assorted Divine Treasures) from Ishikagami Shrine are worshipped here. According to tradition they were rescued during Nobunaga’s burning of Ishikagami (1573), hidden by unknown protectors, dedicated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the “Ikitama no Mori,” lost during the 1867 Ôkage‐mairi frenzy, later recovered from a secondhand shop by Mr Kobayashi of Kire, entrusted through the Asai clan to this shrine in the early Shōwa period when a special hall was built.真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==Cultural Designations== ===Osaka City Designated Tangible Cultural Property=== * Main Hall – early Edo period (1615–1623); designated 2011. ==Annual Events== * Feb 3 (Setsubun): Goma ritual by Sugiyama kō yamabushi in front of the shrine. * Feb 20: Kinensai (prayer for good harvest) – historically observed. * Apr 1: School entrance ceremonies held at the shrine through the Edo period. * Jul first Sunday: Summer festival with mikoshi processions (until ca. 1965 children’s taiko drumming). * Aug 23–24: Jizō‐bon ceremonies, Goma dance in precincts. * Oct 14–15: Autumn festival. * Dec 23: Community shimenawa and tōrō decoration, major cleaning, replacing of old ornaments. ==Kire Village Documents== The “Settsu Province Sumiyoshi District Kire Village Documents,” 38 items dated 1674–1829 plus three early Meiji documents, assembled by Professor Tsuda Hideo, show village‐state relations over shrine land and administration, including petitions in 1870 for clarifying Shinto priesthood roles after shinbutsu bunri.長谷川, 2011, p. 73–88. ==Family Record of Kitamura Family== A 14th‐century genealogy preserved until 1615, recounting ancestral myth and shrine founding from age of Takemikazuchi through Jimmu’s Eastern Expedition, with notes on transformation of place names (Ōtsuka, Tatehara, Mishiragi, etc.). Scholars debate its reliability but note valuable local traditions.井上, 1922, p. 166; 奥野, 1941, p. 69–70; 今井, 1959, p. 9–11; 田中, 1983, p. 210–214. ==Poetry== “Haiku: Hatsumago ni / haya Tatehara no / nohori kana” – Inoue Genzō名葦探杖. “Yozakura hanayagu / Tatehara Jinja ni / kei ke” – Hirano‐ku Iroha Karuta平野区いろはかるた. ==Miscellaneous== * The old shrine site in present‐day Kire Nishi 1-chōme was a marsh‐surrounded cape controlling water transport from Naniwa Palace.歴史案内板6. * During Edo period called Tachihara-no-miya, Tachihara Taki-no-Kami, etc.; site bore traces of a Kofun plateau until early 20th century. * The straight street from torii to Bakura Jizō was once a yabusame course. * A stone pillar inscribed "Okinaga Mawatari no Onna" discovered in 1904 stands beside the Totsukasa hall. * Rice Riot of 1922: shrine precinct served as gathering point; suffered damage worth ¥7. * Former belfry removed in WWII; bell now hangs in ema hall. * From 1947, rotating community shimenawa-making on December 25 (later Dec 23). * Registered as Osaka City Urban Landscape Resource in 2012. * Since 2014: annual children’s mochi-pounding festival with sumo wrestlers. * Since 2015: "Kire Tomoshibi no Yube" lantern festival around shrine precincts. ==Location== '''Address''': 6-1-38 Kire, Hirano-ku, Osaka-shi, Osaka Prefecture 547-0013 '''Access''': 9-minute walk from Kire‐Uriwari Station. '''Nearby''': * Nyoigan‐ji Temple * Osaka Municipal Kire Elementary School * Osaka Kyoiku University Special Needs School ==Notes== {{Reflist|group="注"}} ==References== * 東成郡誌, 1922 * 米騒動の研究 第2巻, 1959 * 大阪府全志 巻之3, 1922 * 息長氏異聞, 1959 * 神社を中心とする村落生活調査報告 1, 2007 * 聖徳太子信仰の成立, 1983 * 津田秀夫文庫文書目録8, 2011 * 平野区誌, 2005 * 式内社調査報告 第5巻, 1977 ==External Links== * [https://www.jinjacho-osaka.net/funai_jinja/dai9shibu/hirano-ku/t115.html Osaka Prefecture Shrine Office] * [https://www.houjin-bangou.nta.go.jp/henkorireki-johoto.html?selHouzinNo=2120005001855 National Tax Agency Corporate Number Database] * [http://kiresonsi.web.fc2.com/index.html Kire Village History Association] [[Category:completion tier 1]] {{translated page|ja|式内楯原神社|version=99478748|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Settsu Province]] [[Category:Son-sha in Osaka Prefecture]] }} [[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]] [[ja:式内楯原神社]] [[de:Shikinai Tatehara Jinja]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Osaka]] [[Category:Son-sha in Osaka Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings in Hirano-ku, Osaka]] [[Category:History of Hirano Ward]] [[Category:pages without english wikidata name]] [[en:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]]

According to tradition they were rescued during Nobunaga’s burning of Ishikagami (1573), hidden by unknown protectors, dedicated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the “Ikitama no Mori,” lost during the 1867 Ôkage‐mairi frenzy, later recovered from a secondhand shop by Mr Kobayashi of Kire, entrusted through the Asai clan to this shrine in the early Shōwa period when a special hall was built.真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==Cultural Designations== ===Osaka City Designated Tangible Cultural Property=== * Main Hall – early Edo period (1615–1623); designated 2011. ==Annual Events== * Feb 3 (Setsubun): Goma ritual by Sugiyama kō yamabushi in front of the shrine. * Feb 20: Kinensai (prayer for good harvest) – historically observed. * Apr 1: School entrance ceremonies held at the shrine through the Edo period. * Jul first Sunday: Summer festival with mikoshi processions (until ca. 1965 children’s taiko drumming). * Aug 23–24: Jizō‐bon ceremonies, Goma dance in precincts. * Oct 14–15: Autumn festival. * Dec 23: Community shimenawa and tōrō decoration, major cleaning, replacing of old ornaments. ==Kire Village Documents== The “Settsu Province Sumiyoshi District Kire Village Documents,” 38 items dated 1674–1829 plus three early Meiji documents, assembled by Professor Tsuda Hideo, show village‐state relations over shrine land and administration, including petitions in 1870 for clarifying Shinto priesthood roles after shinbutsu bunri.長谷川, 2011, p. 73–88. ==Family Record of Kitamura Family== A 14th‐century genealogy preserved until 1615, recounting ancestral myth and shrine founding from age of Takemikazuchi through Jimmu’s Eastern Expedition, with notes on transformation of place names (Ōtsuka, Tatehara, Mishiragi, etc.). Scholars debate its reliability but note valuable local traditions.井上, 1922, p. 166; 奥野, 1941, p. 69–70; 今井, 1959, p. 9–11; 田中, 1983, p. 210–214. ==Poetry== “Haiku: Hatsumago ni / haya Tatehara no / nohori kana” – Inoue Genzō名葦探杖. “Yozakura hanayagu / Tatehara Jinja ni / kei ke” – Hirano‐ku Iroha Karuta平野区いろはかるた. ==Miscellaneous== * The old shrine site in present‐day Kire Nishi 1-chōme was a marsh‐surrounded cape controlling water transport from Naniwa Palace.歴史案内板6. * During Edo period called Tachihara-no-miya, Tachihara Taki-no-Kami, etc.; site bore traces of a Kofun plateau until early 20th century. * The straight street from torii to Bakura Jizō was once a yabusame course. * A stone pillar inscribed "Okinaga Mawatari no Onna" discovered in 1904 stands beside the Totsukasa hall. * Rice Riot of 1922: shrine precinct served as gathering point; suffered damage worth ¥7. * Former belfry removed in WWII; bell now hangs in ema hall. * From 1947, rotating community shimenawa-making on December 25 (later Dec 23). * Registered as Osaka City Urban Landscape Resource in 2012. * Since 2014: annual children’s mochi-pounding festival with sumo wrestlers. * Since 2015: "Kire Tomoshibi no Yube" lantern festival around shrine precincts. ==Location== '''Address''': 6-1-38 Kire, Hirano-ku, Osaka-shi, Osaka Prefecture 547-0013 '''Access''': 9-minute walk from Kire‐Uriwari Station. It is listed in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as a Shikinaisha (small). Under the prewar Ranking system it was classified as a Village Shrine (sonsha), and today it is an independent shrine not affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō). The shrine is identified with the same-named entry for Settsu Province, Sumiyoshi District, in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō. Its main annual festival is held on October 15. ==Deities== * Takemikazuchi no Ōkami * Ōkuninushi no Ōkami * Emperor Kōgen * Sugawara no Michizane * Akaruhime no Mikoto These five deities are enshrined todayFrom the shrine brochure.. Over the centuries there have been multiple mergers and differing records: * Naoashitanjō: Sukuna-Bikona no Mikoto大阪府神社史資料, 1933, p. 737. * Settsu Meisho Zue: same as Sumiyoshi’s Tategozen Shrine?大日本名所図会, 1919, p. 116. * Jinja Kakuryōku: unknown神社覈録 上編, 1902, p. 563. * Tetsusen Shinmeichō: Akaruhime no Mikoto特選神名牒, 1925, p. 138. * Osaka-fu-shi: unknown (theory: Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime)大阪府誌, 1903, p. 198. * Osaka-shi shiseki meishō tennen kinenbutsu: unknown or Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime, or Takemikazuchi大阪府史蹟名勝天然記念物, 1931, p. 37. * Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten & Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei: Takemikazuchi, Sugawara no Michizane, Ōkuninushi, Susanoo no Mikoto, Totsukasa no Ōkami ==Annual Festivals== * Summer Festival: July 5真弓, 1977, p. 259. * Autumn Festival: October 15真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==History== ===Founding=== In Year 6 of Emperor Sujin, the kokuzō (provincial governor) Namuchi no Naki Kuro was ordered by imperial edict to separate the worship of Kuninari no Ōkami and Takemikazuchi no Mikoto, which had been enshrined together, building a distinct hall for Takemikazuchi called Tate no Gozen Shrine and one for Kuninari’s halberd called Hoko no Gozen Shrine. The enshrinement ceremony took place on September 2 of Year 7摂津名所図会; 特選神名牒; 東成郡誌, 1922, p. 1323.. In Year 9 the shrine’s estate boundaries were defined from Taji to Mihara to Naniwa. According to tradition, Kunihira’s halberd was the “Amano-hirohoko” renamed “Kunihira no Hoko” by Ōkuninushi, prophesied to pacify the land when carried. Takemikazuchi brought Ōkuninushi’s spirit into the halberd during the Tenson kōrin, remaining in this area upon pacifying the world. On his deathbed he entrusted his grandson Ō Ōdo no Mikoto to enshrine his Tenka-kusa-no-Tsurugi and the Kunihira no Hoko as his spirit vessels. That grandson aided Emperor Jimmu during the Eastern Expedition with the divine bird Ōtori and was granted the hereditary title of Ken-shin and the name Dadai no Ōdo no Kuni. ===Empress Jingū’s Expedition=== During Empress Jingū’s campaign against the Three Kingdoms of Korea, military oracle rites were received here. On her return in Year 11 of Jingū, she personally worshipped here with Emperor Ōjin (as Prince Hondawake), served by the Ō Ōdo clan. The shrines were renamed Tatehara Jingū and the clan took the name Okinaga.真弓, 1977, p. 257. In Year 62 the crown prince again worshipped and returned the Kunihira no Hoko to Yamato, planting a pine called Mihoko-matsu in its place. ===Genealogy of Emperors and the Okinaga Clan=== [Content tracing the complex legendary lineage from Emperor Sujin through Emperor Keitai and beyond, matching the original with references to Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.] ===Asuka through Heian Periods=== * 607: Imperial envoy Nakatomi no Kamako visits; chrysanthemum crest granted. * Emperor Ichijō donates a suigatsu plaque (gaku). * 1336 (Engen 2): Crown Prince Moriyoshi stays here during his visit, establishing a temporary palace and the arrow‐returning ritual “Yagaeshi no Shinji.” The shrine and palace were later burned by Northern Court forces. * 1481 (Bunmei 13): Shrine relocated to present site. * 1493 (Meiō 2): Major reconstruction of shrine buildings. * Early 1600s: Windstorm damage leads to building anew, consolidating minor shrines such as Ryūō and Tenjin among others. * 1872 (Meiji 5): Tenjin Shrine failed to receive village‐shrine status due to name confusion; Tatehara Shrine (the original) became village shrine. * 1907 (Meiji 40): Merged with Higashi‐Nishi Shrine and Kasuga Shrine under imperial consolidation orders on September 12. * 1910 (Meiji 43): To preserve the name Tatehara, three shrines (Tenjin, Higashi‐Nishi, Kasuga) were re-merged into Tatehara Shrine on December 9. * 1908 (Meiji 41): Designated a Shinsen‐heihaku kyōshinsha. * 1951 (Shōwa 26): East Kire community revived Higashi‐Nishi and Kasuga as Yasaka Shrine, separating them again. ====Alternative account==== ['''Tōsei-gun-shi'''] offers a different post-Meiji consolidation sequence, naming conventions, and shrine merges.大阪府東成郡誌, 1922, pp. 1322–1323. ==Shrine Complex== * Main Hall (Honden): 1-bay Nagare-zukuri, copper plate roof (originally hinoki bark), structural dimensions 2½ ken x 1½ ken; According to tradition they were rescued during Nobunaga’s burning of Ishikagami (1573), hidden by unknown protectors, dedicated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the “Ikitama no Mori,” lost during the 1867 Ôkage‐mairi frenzy, later recovered from a secondhand shop by Mr Kobayashi of Kire, entrusted through the Asai clan to this shrine in the early Shōwa period when a special hall was built.真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==Cultural Designations== ===Osaka City Designated Tangible Cultural Property=== * Main Hall – early Edo period (1615–1623); designated 2011. ==Annual Events== * Feb 3 (Setsubun): Goma ritual by Sugiyama kō yamabushi in front of the shrine. * Feb 20: Kinensai (prayer for good harvest) – historically observed. * Apr 1: School entrance ceremonies held at the shrine through the Edo period. * Jul first Sunday: Summer festival with mikoshi processions (until ca. 1965 children’s taiko drumming). * Aug 23–24: Jizō‐bon ceremonies, Goma dance in precincts. * Oct 14–15: Autumn festival. * Dec 23: Community shimenawa and tōrō decoration, major cleaning, replacing of old ornaments. ==Kire Village Documents== The “Settsu Province Sumiyoshi District Kire Village Documents,” 38 items dated 1674–1829 plus three early Meiji documents, assembled by Professor Tsuda Hideo, show village‐state relations over shrine land and administration, including petitions in 1870 for clarifying Shinto priesthood roles after shinbutsu bunri.長谷川, 2011, p. 73–88. ==Family Record of Kitamura Family== A 14th‐century genealogy preserved until 1615, recounting ancestral myth and shrine founding from age of Takemikazuchi through Jimmu’s Eastern Expedition, with notes on transformation of place names (Ōtsuka, Tatehara, Mishiragi, etc.). Scholars debate its reliability but note valuable local traditions.井上, 1922, p. 166; 奥野, 1941, p. 69–70; 今井, 1959, p. 9–11; 田中, 1983, p. 210–214. ==Poetry== “Haiku: Hatsumago ni / haya Tatehara no / nohori kana” – Inoue Genzō名葦探杖. “Yozakura hanayagu / Tatehara Jinja ni / kei ke” – Hirano‐ku Iroha Karuta平野区いろはかるた. ==Miscellaneous== * The old shrine site in present‐day Kire Nishi 1-chōme was a marsh‐surrounded cape controlling water transport from Naniwa Palace.歴史案内板6. * During Edo period called Tachihara-no-miya, Tachihara Taki-no-Kami, etc.; site bore traces of a Kofun plateau until early 20th century. * The straight street from torii to Bakura Jizō was once a yabusame course. * A stone pillar inscribed "Okinaga Mawatari no Onna" discovered in 1904 stands beside the Totsukasa hall. * Rice Riot of 1922: shrine precinct served as gathering point; suffered damage worth ¥7. * Former belfry removed in WWII; bell now hangs in ema hall. * From 1947, rotating community shimenawa-making on December 25 (later Dec 23). * Registered as Osaka City Urban Landscape Resource in 2012. * Since 2014: annual children’s mochi-pounding festival with sumo wrestlers. * Since 2015: "Kire Tomoshibi no Yube" lantern festival around shrine precincts. ==Location== '''Address''': 6-1-38 Kire, Hirano-ku, Osaka-shi, Osaka Prefecture 547-0013 '''Access''': 9-minute walk from Kire‐Uriwari Station. It is listed in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as a Shikinaisha (small). Under the prewar Ranking system it was classified as a Village Shrine (sonsha), and today it is an independent shrine not affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō). The shrine is identified with the same-named entry for Settsu Province, Sumiyoshi District, in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō. Its main annual festival is held on October 15. ==Deities== * Takemikazuchi no Ōkami * Ōkuninushi no Ōkami * Emperor Kōgen * Sugawara no Michizane * Akaruhime no Mikoto These five deities are enshrined todayFrom the shrine brochure.. Over the centuries there have been multiple mergers and differing records: * Naoashitanjō: Sukuna-Bikona no Mikoto大阪府神社史資料, 1933, p. 737. * Settsu Meisho Zue: same as Sumiyoshi’s Tategozen Shrine?大日本名所図会, 1919, p. 116. * Jinja Kakuryōku: unknown神社覈録 上編, 1902, p. 563. * Tetsusen Shinmeichō: Akaruhime no Mikoto特選神名牒, 1925, p. 138. * Osaka-fu-shi: unknown (theory: Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime)大阪府誌, 1903, p. 198. * Osaka-shi shiseki meishō tennen kinenbutsu: unknown or Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime, or Takemikazuchi大阪府史蹟名勝天然記念物, 1931, p. 37. * Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten & Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei: Takemikazuchi, Sugawara no Michizane, Ōkuninushi, Susanoo no Mikoto, Totsukasa no Ōkami ==Annual Festivals== * Summer Festival: July 5真弓, 1977, p. 259. * Autumn Festival: October 15真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==History== ===Founding=== In Year 6 of Emperor Sujin, the kokuzō (provincial governor) Namuchi no Naki Kuro was ordered by imperial edict to separate the worship of Kuninari no Ōkami and Takemikazuchi no Mikoto, which had been enshrined together, building a distinct hall for Takemikazuchi called Tate no Gozen Shrine and one for Kuninari’s halberd called Hoko no Gozen Shrine. The enshrinement ceremony took place on September 2 of Year 7摂津名所図会; 特選神名牒; 東成郡誌, 1922, p. 1323.. In Year 9 the shrine’s estate boundaries were defined from Taji to Mihara to Naniwa. According to tradition, Kunihira’s halberd was the “Amano-hirohoko” renamed “Kunihira no Hoko” by Ōkuninushi, prophesied to pacify the land when carried. Takemikazuchi brought Ōkuninushi’s spirit into the halberd during the Tenson kōrin, remaining in this area upon pacifying the world. On his deathbed he entrusted his grandson Ō Ōdo no Mikoto to enshrine his Tenka-kusa-no-Tsurugi and the Kunihira no Hoko as his spirit vessels. That grandson aided Emperor Jimmu during the Eastern Expedition with the divine bird Ōtori and was granted the hereditary title of Ken-shin and the name Dadai no Ōdo no Kuni. ===Empress Jingū’s Expedition=== During Empress Jingū’s campaign against the Three Kingdoms of Korea, military oracle rites were received here. On her return in Year 11 of Jingū, she personally worshipped here with Emperor Ōjin (as Prince Hondawake), served by the Ō Ōdo clan. The shrines were renamed Tatehara Jingū and the clan took the name Okinaga.真弓, 1977, p. 257. In Year 62 the crown prince again worshipped and returned the Kunihira no Hoko to Yamato, planting a pine called Mihoko-matsu in its place. ===Genealogy of Emperors and the Okinaga Clan=== [Content tracing the complex legendary lineage from Emperor Sujin through Emperor Keitai and beyond, matching the original with references to Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.] ===Asuka through Heian Periods=== * 607: Imperial envoy Nakatomi no Kamako visits; chrysanthemum crest granted. * Emperor Ichijō donates a suigatsu plaque (gaku). * 1336 (Engen 2): Crown Prince Moriyoshi stays here during his visit, establishing a temporary palace and the arrow‐returning ritual “Yagaeshi no Shinji.” The shrine and palace were later burned by Northern Court forces. * 1481 (Bunmei 13): Shrine relocated to present site. * 1493 (Meiō 2): Major reconstruction of shrine buildings. * Early 1600s: Windstorm damage leads to building anew, consolidating minor shrines such as Ryūō and Tenjin among others. * 1872 (Meiji 5): Tenjin Shrine failed to receive village‐shrine status due to name confusion; Tatehara Shrine (the original) became village shrine. * 1907 (Meiji 40): Merged with Higashi‐Nishi Shrine and Kasuga Shrine under imperial consolidation orders on September 12. * 1910 (Meiji 43): To preserve the name Tatehara, three shrines (Tenjin, Higashi‐Nishi, Kasuga) were re-merged into Tatehara Shrine on December 9. * 1908 (Meiji 41): Designated a Shinsen‐heihaku kyōshinsha. * 1951 (Shōwa 26): East Kire community revived Higashi‐Nishi and Kasuga as Yasaka Shrine, separating them again. ====Alternative account==== ['''Tōsei-gun-shi'''] offers a different post-Meiji consolidation sequence, naming conventions, and shrine merges.大阪府東成郡誌, 1922, pp. 1322–1323. ==Shrine Complex== * Main Hall (Honden): 1-bay Nagare-zukuri, copper plate roof (originally hinoki bark), structural dimensions 2½ ken x 1½ ken; '''Nearby''': * Nyoigan‐ji Temple * Osaka Municipal Kire Elementary School * Osaka Kyoiku University Special Needs School ==Notes== {{Reflist|group="注"}} ==References== * 東成郡誌, 1922 * 米騒動の研究 第2巻, 1959 * 大阪府全志 巻之3, 1922 * 息長氏異聞, 1959 * 神社を中心とする村落生活調査報告 1, 2007 * 聖徳太子信仰の成立, 1983 * 津田秀夫文庫文書目録8, 2011 * 平野区誌, 2005 * 式内社調査報告 第5巻, 1977 ==External Links== * [https://www.jinjacho-osaka.net/funai_jinja/dai9shibu/hirano-ku/t115.html Osaka Prefecture Shrine Office] * [https://www.houjin-bangou.nta.go.jp/henkorireki-johoto.html?selHouzinNo=2120005001855 National Tax Agency Corporate Number Database] * [http://kiresonsi.web.fc2.com/index.html Kire Village History Association] [[Category:completion tier 1]] {{translated page|ja|式内楯原神社|version=99478748|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Settsu Province]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[Category:qq]] [[Category:Son-sha in Osaka Prefecture]] }} [[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]] [[ja:式内楯原神社]] [[de:Shikinai Tatehara Jinja]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Osaka]] [[Category:Son-sha in Osaka Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings in Hirano-ku, Osaka]] [[Category:History of Hirano Ward]] [[Category:pages without english wikidata name]] [[en:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]] [[Category:qq]]

According to tradition they were rescued during Nobunaga’s burning of Ishikagami (1573), hidden by unknown protectors, dedicated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the “Ikitama no Mori,” lost during the 1867 Ôkage‐mairi frenzy, later recovered from a secondhand shop by Mr Kobayashi of Kire, entrusted through the Asai clan to this shrine in the early Shōwa period when a special hall was built.真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==Cultural Designations== ===Osaka City Designated Tangible Cultural Property=== * Main Hall – early Edo period (1615–1623); designated 2011. ==Annual Events== * Feb 3 (Setsubun): Goma ritual by Sugiyama kō yamabushi in front of the shrine. * Feb 20: Kinensai (prayer for good harvest) – historically observed. * Apr 1: School entrance ceremonies held at the shrine through the Edo period. * Jul first Sunday: Summer festival with mikoshi processions (until ca. 1965 children’s taiko drumming). * Aug 23–24: Jizō‐bon ceremonies, Goma dance in precincts. * Oct 14–15: Autumn festival. * Dec 23: Community shimenawa and tōrō decoration, major cleaning, replacing of old ornaments. ==Kire Village Documents== The “Settsu Province Sumiyoshi District Kire Village Documents,” 38 items dated 1674–1829 plus three early Meiji documents, assembled by Professor Tsuda Hideo, show village‐state relations over shrine land and administration, including petitions in 1870 for clarifying Shinto priesthood roles after shinbutsu bunri.長谷川, 2011, p. 73–88. ==Family Record of Kitamura Family== A 14th‐century genealogy preserved until 1615, recounting ancestral myth and shrine founding from age of Takemikazuchi through Jimmu’s Eastern Expedition, with notes on transformation of place names (Ōtsuka, Tatehara, Mishiragi, etc.). Scholars debate its reliability but note valuable local traditions.井上, 1922, p. 166; 奥野, 1941, p. 69–70; 今井, 1959, p. 9–11; 田中, 1983, p. 210–214. ==Poetry== “Haiku: Hatsumago ni / haya Tatehara no / nohori kana” – Inoue Genzō名葦探杖. “Yozakura hanayagu / Tatehara Jinja ni / kei ke” – Hirano‐ku Iroha Karuta平野区いろはかるた. ==Miscellaneous== * The old shrine site in present‐day Kire Nishi 1-chōme was a marsh‐surrounded cape controlling water transport from Naniwa Palace.歴史案内板6. * During Edo period called Tachihara-no-miya, Tachihara Taki-no-Kami, etc.; site bore traces of a Kofun plateau until early 20th century. * The straight street from torii to Bakura Jizō was once a yabusame course. * A stone pillar inscribed "Okinaga Mawatari no Onna" discovered in 1904 stands beside the Totsukasa hall. * Rice Riot of 1922: shrine precinct served as gathering point; suffered damage worth ¥7. * Former belfry removed in WWII; bell now hangs in ema hall. * From 1947, rotating community shimenawa-making on December 25 (later Dec 23). * Registered as Osaka City Urban Landscape Resource in 2012. * Since 2014: annual children’s mochi-pounding festival with sumo wrestlers. * Since 2015: "Kire Tomoshibi no Yube" lantern festival around shrine precincts. ==Location== '''Address''': 6-1-38 Kire, Hirano-ku, Osaka-shi, Osaka Prefecture 547-0013 '''Access''': 9-minute walk from Kire‐Uriwari Station. It is listed in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as a Shikinaisha (small). Under the prewar Ranking system it was classified as a Village Shrine (sonsha), and today it is an independent shrine not affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō). The shrine is identified with the same-named entry for Settsu Province, Sumiyoshi District, in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō. Over the centuries there have been multiple mergers and differing records: * Naoashitanjō: Sukuna-Bikona no Mikoto大阪府神社史資料, 1933, p. 737. * Settsu Meisho Zue: same as Sumiyoshi’s Tategozen Shrine?大日本名所図会, 1919, p. 116. * Jinja Kakuryōku: unknown神社覈録 上編, 1902, p. 563. * Tetsusen Shinmeichō: Akaruhime no Mikoto特選神名牒, 1925, p. 138. * Osaka-fu-shi: unknown (theory: Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime)大阪府誌, 1903, p. 198. * Osaka-shi shiseki meishō tennen kinenbutsu: unknown or Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime, or Takemikazuchi大阪府史蹟名勝天然記念物, 1931, p. 37. * Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten & Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei: Takemikazuchi, Sugawara no Michizane, Ōkuninushi, Susanoo no Mikoto, Totsukasa no Ōkami ==Annual Festivals== * Summer Festival: July 5真弓, 1977, p. 259. * Autumn Festival: October 15真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==History== ===Founding=== In Year 6 of Emperor Sujin, the kokuzō (provincial governor) Namuchi no Naki Kuro was ordered by imperial edict to separate the worship of Kuninari no Ōkami and Takemikazuchi no Mikoto, which had been enshrined together, building a distinct hall for Takemikazuchi called Tate no Gozen Shrine and one for Kuninari’s halberd called Hoko no Gozen Shrine. The enshrinement ceremony took place on September 2 of Year 7摂津名所図会; 特選神名牒; 東成郡誌, 1922, p. 1323.. In Year 9 the shrine’s estate boundaries were defined from Taji to Mihara to Naniwa. According to tradition, Kunihira’s halberd was the “Amano-hirohoko” renamed “Kunihira no Hoko” by Ōkuninushi, prophesied to pacify the land when carried. Takemikazuchi brought Ōkuninushi’s spirit into the halberd during the Tenson kōrin, remaining in this area upon pacifying the world. On his deathbed he entrusted his grandson Ō Ōdo no Mikoto to enshrine his Tenka-kusa-no-Tsurugi and the Kunihira no Hoko as his spirit vessels. That grandson aided Emperor Jimmu during the Eastern Expedition with the divine bird Ōtori and was granted the hereditary title of Ken-shin and the name Dadai no Ōdo no Kuni. ===Empress Jingū’s Expedition=== During Empress Jingū’s campaign against the Three Kingdoms of Korea, military oracle rites were received here. On her return in Year 11 of Jingū, she personally worshipped here with Emperor Ōjin (as Prince Hondawake), served by the Ō Ōdo clan. The shrines were renamed Tatehara Jingū and the clan took the name Okinaga.真弓, 1977, p. 257. In Year 62 the crown prince again worshipped and returned the Kunihira no Hoko to Yamato, planting a pine called Mihoko-matsu in its place. ===Genealogy of Emperors and the Okinaga Clan=== [Content tracing the complex legendary lineage from Emperor Sujin through Emperor Keitai and beyond, matching the original with references to Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.] ===Asuka through Heian Periods=== * 607: Imperial envoy Nakatomi no Kamako visits; chrysanthemum crest granted. * Emperor Ichijō donates a suigatsu plaque (gaku). * 1336 (Engen 2): Crown Prince Moriyoshi stays here during his visit, establishing a temporary palace and the arrow‐returning ritual “Yagaeshi no Shinji.” The shrine and palace were later burned by Northern Court forces. * 1481 (Bunmei 13): Shrine relocated to present site. * 1493 (Meiō 2): Major reconstruction of shrine buildings. * Early 1600s: Windstorm damage leads to building anew, consolidating minor shrines such as Ryūō and Tenjin among others. * 1872 (Meiji 5): Tenjin Shrine failed to receive village‐shrine status due to name confusion; Tatehara Shrine (the original) became village shrine. * 1907 (Meiji 40): Merged with Higashi‐Nishi Shrine and Kasuga Shrine under imperial consolidation orders on September 12. * 1910 (Meiji 43): To preserve the name Tatehara, three shrines (Tenjin, Higashi‐Nishi, Kasuga) were re-merged into Tatehara Shrine on December 9. * 1908 (Meiji 41): Designated a Shinsen‐heihaku kyōshinsha. * 1951 (Shōwa 26): East Kire community revived Higashi‐Nishi and Kasuga as Yasaka Shrine, separating them again. ====Alternative account==== ['''Tōsei-gun-shi'''] offers a different post-Meiji consolidation sequence, naming conventions, and shrine merges.大阪府東成郡誌, 1922, pp. 1322–1323. ==Shrine Complex== * Main Hall (Honden): 1-bay Nagare-zukuri, copper plate roof (originally hinoki bark), structural dimensions 2½ ken x 1½ ken; '''Nearby''': * Nyoigan‐ji Temple * Osaka Municipal Kire Elementary School * Osaka Kyoiku University Special Needs School ==Notes== {{Reflist|group="注"}} ==References== * 東成郡誌, 1922 * 米騒動の研究 第2巻, 1959 * 大阪府全志 巻之3, 1922 * 息長氏異聞, 1959 * 神社を中心とする村落生活調査報告 1, 2007 * 聖徳太子信仰の成立, 1983 * 津田秀夫文庫文書目録8, 2011 * 平野区誌, 2005 * 式内社調査報告 第5巻, 1977 ==External Links== * [https://www.jinjacho-osaka.net/funai_jinja/dai9shibu/hirano-ku/t115.html Osaka Prefecture Shrine Office] * [https://www.houjin-bangou.nta.go.jp/henkorireki-johoto.html?selHouzinNo=2120005001855 National Tax Agency Corporate Number Database] * [http://kiresonsi.web.fc2.com/index.html Kire Village History Association] [[Category:completion tier 1]] {{translated page|ja|式内楯原神社|version=99478748|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Settsu Province]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[Category:qq]] [[Category:Son-sha in Osaka Prefecture]] }} [[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]] [[ja:式内楯原神社]] [[de:Shikinai Tatehara Jinja]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Osaka]] [[Category:Son-sha in Osaka Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings in Hirano-ku, Osaka]] [[Category:History of Hirano Ward]] [[Category:pages without english wikidata name]] [[en:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:qq]]

According to tradition they were rescued during Nobunaga’s burning of Ishikagami (1573), hidden by unknown protectors, dedicated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the “Ikitama no Mori,” lost during the 1867 Ôkage‐mairi frenzy, later recovered from a secondhand shop by Mr Kobayashi of Kire, entrusted through the Asai clan to this shrine in the early Shōwa period when a special hall was built.真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==Cultural Designations== ===Osaka City Designated Tangible Cultural Property=== * Main Hall – early Edo period (1615–1623); designated 2011. ==Annual Events== * Feb 3 (Setsubun): Goma ritual by Sugiyama kō yamabushi in front of the shrine. * Feb 20: Kinensai (prayer for good harvest) – historically observed. * Apr 1: School entrance ceremonies held at the shrine through the Edo period. * Jul first Sunday: Summer festival with mikoshi processions (until ca. 1965 children’s taiko drumming). * Aug 23–24: Jizō‐bon ceremonies, Goma dance in precincts. * Oct 14–15: Autumn festival. * Dec 23: Community shimenawa and tōrō decoration, major cleaning, replacing of old ornaments. ==Kire Village Documents== The “Settsu Province Sumiyoshi District Kire Village Documents,” 38 items dated 1674–1829 plus three early Meiji documents, assembled by Professor Tsuda Hideo, show village‐state relations over shrine land and administration, including petitions in 1870 for clarifying Shinto priesthood roles after shinbutsu bunri.長谷川, 2011, p. 73–88. ==Family Record of Kitamura Family== A 14th‐century genealogy preserved until 1615, recounting ancestral myth and shrine founding from age of Takemikazuchi through Jimmu’s Eastern Expedition, with notes on transformation of place names (Ōtsuka, Tatehara, Mishiragi, etc.). It is listed in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as a Shikinaisha (small). Under the prewar Ranking system it was classified as a Village Shrine (sonsha), and today it is an independent shrine not affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō). The shrine is identified with the same-named entry for Settsu Province, Sumiyoshi District, in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō. Over the centuries there have been multiple mergers and differing records: * Naoashitanjō: Sukuna-Bikona no Mikoto大阪府神社史資料, 1933, p. 737. * Settsu Meisho Zue: same as Sumiyoshi’s Tategozen Shrine?大日本名所図会, 1919, p. 116. * Jinja Kakuryōku: unknown神社覈録 上編, 1902, p. 563. * Tetsusen Shinmeichō: Akaruhime no Mikoto特選神名牒, 1925, p. 138. * Osaka-fu-shi: unknown (theory: Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime)大阪府誌, 1903, p. 198. * Osaka-shi shiseki meishō tennen kinenbutsu: unknown or Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime, or Takemikazuchi大阪府史蹟名勝天然記念物, 1931, p. 37. * Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten & Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei: Takemikazuchi, Sugawara no Michizane, Ōkuninushi, Susanoo no Mikoto, Totsukasa no Ōkami ==Annual Festivals== * Summer Festival: July 5真弓, 1977, p. 259. * Autumn Festival: October 15真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==History== ===Founding=== In Year 6 of Emperor Sujin, the kokuzō (provincial governor) Namuchi no Naki Kuro was ordered by imperial edict to separate the worship of Kuninari no Ōkami and Takemikazuchi no Mikoto, which had been enshrined together, building a distinct hall for Takemikazuchi called Tate no Gozen Shrine and one for Kuninari’s halberd called Hoko no Gozen Shrine. The enshrinement ceremony took place on September 2 of Year 7摂津名所図会; 特選神名牒; 東成郡誌, 1922, p. 1323.. In Year 9 the shrine’s estate boundaries were defined from Taji to Mihara to Naniwa. According to tradition, Kunihira’s halberd was the “Amano-hirohoko” renamed “Kunihira no Hoko” by Ōkuninushi, prophesied to pacify the land when carried. Takemikazuchi brought Ōkuninushi’s spirit into the halberd during the Tenson kōrin, remaining in this area upon pacifying the world. On his deathbed he entrusted his grandson Ō Ōdo no Mikoto to enshrine his Tenka-kusa-no-Tsurugi and the Kunihira no Hoko as his spirit vessels. That grandson aided Emperor Jimmu during the Eastern Expedition with the divine bird Ōtori and was granted the hereditary title of Ken-shin and the name Dadai no Ōdo no Kuni. ===Empress Jingū’s Expedition=== During Empress Jingū’s campaign against the Three Kingdoms of Korea, military oracle rites were received here. On her return in Year 11 of Jingū, she personally worshipped here with Emperor Ōjin (as Prince Hondawake), served by the Ō Ōdo clan. The shrines were renamed Tatehara Jingū and the clan took the name Okinaga.真弓, 1977, p. 257. In Year 62 the crown prince again worshipped and returned the Kunihira no Hoko to Yamato, planting a pine called Mihoko-matsu in its place. ===Genealogy of Emperors and the Okinaga Clan=== [Content tracing the complex legendary lineage from Emperor Sujin through Emperor Keitai and beyond, matching the original with references to Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.] ===Asuka through Heian Periods=== * 607: Imperial envoy Nakatomi no Kamako visits; chrysanthemum crest granted. * Emperor Ichijō donates a suigatsu plaque (gaku). * 1336 (Engen 2): Crown Prince Moriyoshi stays here during his visit, establishing a temporary palace and the arrow‐returning ritual “Yagaeshi no Shinji.” The shrine and palace were later burned by Northern Court forces. * 1481 (Bunmei 13): Shrine relocated to present site. * 1493 (Meiō 2): Major reconstruction of shrine buildings. * Early 1600s: Windstorm damage leads to building anew, consolidating minor shrines such as Ryūō and Tenjin among others. * 1872 (Meiji 5): Tenjin Shrine failed to receive village‐shrine status due to name confusion; Tatehara Shrine (the original) became village shrine. * 1907 (Meiji 40): Merged with Higashi‐Nishi Shrine and Kasuga Shrine under imperial consolidation orders on September 12. * 1910 (Meiji 43): To preserve the name Tatehara, three shrines (Tenjin, Higashi‐Nishi, Kasuga) were re-merged into Tatehara Shrine on December 9. * 1908 (Meiji 41): Designated a Shinsen‐heihaku kyōshinsha. * 1951 (Shōwa 26): East Kire community revived Higashi‐Nishi and Kasuga as Yasaka Shrine, separating them again. ====Alternative account==== ['''Tōsei-gun-shi'''] offers a different post-Meiji consolidation sequence, naming conventions, and shrine merges.大阪府東成郡誌, 1922, pp. 1322–1323. ==Shrine Complex== * Main Hall (Honden): 1-bay Nagare-zukuri, copper plate roof (originally hinoki bark), structural dimensions 2½ ken x 1½ ken; According to tradition they were rescued during Nobunaga’s burning of Ishikagami (1573), hidden by unknown protectors, dedicated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the “Ikitama no Mori,” lost during the 1867 Ôkage‐mairi frenzy, later recovered from a secondhand shop by Mr Kobayashi of Kire, entrusted through the Asai clan to this shrine in the early Shōwa period when a special hall was built.真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==Cultural Designations== ===Osaka City Designated Tangible Cultural Property=== * Main Hall – early Edo period (1615–1623); designated 2011. ==Annual Events== * Feb 3 (Setsubun): Goma ritual by Sugiyama kō yamabushi in front of the shrine. * Feb 20: Kinensai (prayer for good harvest) – historically observed. * Apr 1: School entrance ceremonies held at the shrine through the Edo period. * Jul first Sunday: Summer festival with mikoshi processions (until ca. 1965 children’s taiko drumming). * Aug 23–24: Jizō‐bon ceremonies, Goma dance in precincts. * Oct 14–15: Autumn festival. * Dec 23: Community shimenawa and tōrō decoration, major cleaning, replacing of old ornaments. ==Kire Village Documents== The “Settsu Province Sumiyoshi District Kire Village Documents,” 38 items dated 1674–1829 plus three early Meiji documents, assembled by Professor Tsuda Hideo, show village‐state relations over shrine land and administration, including petitions in 1870 for clarifying Shinto priesthood roles after shinbutsu bunri.長谷川, 2011, p. 73–88. ==Family Record of Kitamura Family== A 14th‐century genealogy preserved until 1615, recounting ancestral myth and shrine founding from age of Takemikazuchi through Jimmu’s Eastern Expedition, with notes on transformation of place names (Ōtsuka, Tatehara, Mishiragi, etc.). It is listed in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as a Shikinaisha (small). Under the prewar Ranking system it was classified as a Village Shrine (sonsha), and today it is an independent shrine not affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō). The enshrinement ceremony took place on September 2 of Year 7摂津名所図会; 特選神名牒; 東成郡誌, 1922, p. 1323.. In Year 9 the shrine’s estate boundaries were defined from Taji to Mihara to Naniwa. According to tradition, Kunihira’s halberd was the “Amano-hirohoko” renamed “Kunihira no Hoko” by Ōkuninushi, prophesied to pacify the land when carried. Takemikazuchi brought Ōkuninushi’s spirit into the halberd during the Tenson kōrin, remaining in this area upon pacifying the world. On his deathbed he entrusted his grandson Ō Ōdo no Mikoto to enshrine his Tenka-kusa-no-Tsurugi and the Kunihira no Hoko as his spirit vessels. That grandson aided Emperor Jimmu during the Eastern Expedition with the divine bird Ōtori and was granted the hereditary title of Ken-shin and the name Dadai no Ōdo no Kuni. ===Empress Jingū’s Expedition=== During Empress Jingū’s campaign against the Three Kingdoms of Korea, military oracle rites were received here. On her return in Year 11 of Jingū, she personally worshipped here with Emperor Ōjin (as Prince Hondawake), served by the Ō Ōdo clan. The shrines were renamed Tatehara Jingū and the clan took the name Okinaga.真弓, 1977, p. 257. In Year 62 the crown prince again worshipped and returned the Kunihira no Hoko to Yamato, planting a pine called Mihoko-matsu in its place. ===Genealogy of Emperors and the Okinaga Clan=== [Content tracing the complex legendary lineage from Emperor Sujin through Emperor Keitai and beyond, matching the original with references to Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.] ===Asuka through Heian Periods=== * 607: Imperial envoy Nakatomi no Kamako visits; chrysanthemum crest granted. * Emperor Ichijō donates a suigatsu plaque (gaku). * 1336 (Engen 2): Crown Prince Moriyoshi stays here during his visit, establishing a temporary palace and the arrow‐returning ritual “Yagaeshi no Shinji.” The shrine and palace were later burned by Northern Court forces. * 1481 (Bunmei 13): Shrine relocated to present site. * 1493 (Meiō 2): Major reconstruction of shrine buildings. * Early 1600s: Windstorm damage leads to building anew, consolidating minor shrines such as Ryūō and Tenjin among others. * 1872 (Meiji 5): Tenjin Shrine failed to receive village‐shrine status due to name confusion; Tatehara Shrine (the original) became village shrine. * 1907 (Meiji 40): Merged with Higashi‐Nishi Shrine and Kasuga Shrine under imperial consolidation orders on September 12. * 1910 (Meiji 43): To preserve the name Tatehara, three shrines (Tenjin, Higashi‐Nishi, Kasuga) were re-merged into Tatehara Shrine on December 9. * 1908 (Meiji 41): Designated a Shinsen‐heihaku kyōshinsha. * 1951 (Shōwa 26): East Kire community revived Higashi‐Nishi and Kasuga as Yasaka Shrine, separating them again. ====Alternative account==== ['''Tōsei-gun-shi'''] offers a different post-Meiji consolidation sequence, naming conventions, and shrine merges.大阪府東成郡誌, 1922, pp. 1322–1323. ==Shrine Complex== * Main Hall (Honden): 1-bay Nagare-zukuri, copper plate roof (originally hinoki bark), structural dimensions 2½ ken x 1½ ken; According to tradition they were rescued during Nobunaga’s burning of Ishikagami (1573), hidden by unknown protectors, dedicated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the “Ikitama no Mori,” lost during the 1867 Ôkage‐mairi frenzy, later recovered from a secondhand shop by Mr Kobayashi of Kire, entrusted through the Asai clan to this shrine in the early Shōwa period when a special hall was built.真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==Cultural Designations== ===Osaka City Designated Tangible Cultural Property=== * Main Hall – early Edo period (1615–1623); designated 2011. ==Annual Events== * Feb 3 (Setsubun): Goma ritual by Sugiyama kō yamabushi in front of the shrine. * Feb 20: Kinensai (prayer for good harvest) – historically observed. * Apr 1: School entrance ceremonies held at the shrine through the Edo period. * Jul first Sunday: Summer festival with mikoshi processions (until ca. 1965 children’s taiko drumming). * Aug 23–24: Jizō‐bon ceremonies, Goma dance in precincts. * Oct 14–15: Autumn festival. * Dec 23: Community shimenawa and tōrō decoration, major cleaning, replacing of old ornaments. ==Kire Village Documents== The “Settsu Province Sumiyoshi District Kire Village Documents,” 38 items dated 1674–1829 plus three early Meiji documents, assembled by Professor Tsuda Hideo, show village‐state relations over shrine land and administration, including petitions in 1870 for clarifying Shinto priesthood roles after shinbutsu bunri.長谷川, 2011, p. 73–88. ==Family Record of Kitamura Family== A 14th‐century genealogy preserved until 1615, recounting ancestral myth and shrine founding from age of Takemikazuchi through Jimmu’s Eastern Expedition, with notes on transformation of place names (Ōtsuka, Tatehara, Mishiragi, etc.). Scholars debate its reliability but note valuable local traditions.井上, 1922, p. 166; 奥野, 1941, p. 69–70; 今井, 1959, p. 9–11; 田中, 1983, p. 210–214. ==Poetry== “Haiku: Hatsumago ni / haya Tatehara no / nohori kana” – Inoue Genzō名葦探杖. “Yozakura hanayagu / Tatehara Jinja ni / kei ke” – Hirano‐ku Iroha Karuta平野区いろはかるた. ==Miscellaneous== * The old shrine site in present‐day Kire Nishi 1-chōme was a marsh‐surrounded cape controlling water transport from Naniwa Palace.歴史案内板6. * During Edo period called Tachihara-no-miya, Tachihara Taki-no-Kami, etc.; site bore traces of a Kofun plateau until early 20th century. * The straight street from torii to Bakura Jizō was once a yabusame course. * A stone pillar inscribed "Okinaga Mawatari no Onna" discovered in 1904 stands beside the Totsukasa hall. * Rice Riot of 1922: shrine precinct served as gathering point; suffered damage worth ¥7. * Former belfry removed in WWII; bell now hangs in ema hall. * From 1947, rotating community shimenawa-making on December 25 (later Dec 23). * Registered as Osaka City Urban Landscape Resource in 2012. * Since 2014: annual children’s mochi-pounding festival with sumo wrestlers. * Since 2015: "Kire Tomoshibi no Yube" lantern festival around shrine precincts. ==Location== '''Address''': 6-1-38 Kire, Hirano-ku, Osaka-shi, Osaka Prefecture 547-0013 '''Access''': 9-minute walk from Kire‐Uriwari Station. It is listed in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as a Shikinaisha (small). Under the prewar Ranking system it was classified as a Village Shrine (sonsha), and today it is an independent shrine not affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō). The shrine is identified with the same-named entry for Settsu Province, Sumiyoshi District, in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō. Its main annual festival is held on October 15. ==Deities== * Takemikazuchi no Ōkami * Ōkuninushi no Ōkami * Emperor Kōgen * Sugawara no Michizane * Akaruhime no Mikoto These five deities are enshrined todayFrom the shrine brochure.. Over the centuries there have been multiple mergers and differing records: * Naoashitanjō: Sukuna-Bikona no Mikoto大阪府神社史資料, 1933, p. 737. * Settsu Meisho Zue: same as Sumiyoshi’s Tategozen Shrine?大日本名所図会, 1919, p. 116. * Jinja Kakuryōku: unknown神社覈録 上編, 1902, p. 563. * Tetsusen Shinmeichō: Akaruhime no Mikoto特選神名牒, 1925, p. 138. * Osaka-fu-shi: unknown (theory: Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime)大阪府誌, 1903, p. 198. * Osaka-shi shiseki meishō tennen kinenbutsu: unknown or Toyotamahiko, Akaruhime, Toyotamahime, or Takemikazuchi大阪府史蹟名勝天然記念物, 1931, p. 37. * Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten & Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei: Takemikazuchi, Sugawara no Michizane, Ōkuninushi, Susanoo no Mikoto, Totsukasa no Ōkami ==Annual Festivals== * Summer Festival: July 5真弓, 1977, p. 259. * Autumn Festival: October 15真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==History== ===Founding=== In Year 6 of Emperor Sujin, the kokuzō (provincial governor) Namuchi no Naki Kuro was ordered by imperial edict to separate the worship of Kuninari no Ōkami and Takemikazuchi no Mikoto, which had been enshrined together, building a distinct hall for Takemikazuchi called Tate no Gozen Shrine and one for Kuninari’s halberd called Hoko no Gozen Shrine. The enshrinement ceremony took place on September 2 of Year 7摂津名所図会; 特選神名牒; 東成郡誌, 1922, p. 1323.. In Year 9 the shrine’s estate boundaries were defined from Taji to Mihara to Naniwa. According to tradition, Kunihira’s halberd was the “Amano-hirohoko” renamed “Kunihira no Hoko” by Ōkuninushi, prophesied to pacify the land when carried. Takemikazuchi brought Ōkuninushi’s spirit into the halberd during the Tenson kōrin, remaining in this area upon pacifying the world. On his deathbed he entrusted his grandson Ō Ōdo no Mikoto to enshrine his Tenka-kusa-no-Tsurugi and the Kunihira no Hoko as his spirit vessels. That grandson aided Emperor Jimmu during the Eastern Expedition with the divine bird Ōtori and was granted the hereditary title of Ken-shin and the name Dadai no Ōdo no Kuni. ===Empress Jingū’s Expedition=== During Empress Jingū’s campaign against the Three Kingdoms of Korea, military oracle rites were received here. On her return in Year 11 of Jingū, she personally worshipped here with Emperor Ōjin (as Prince Hondawake), served by the Ō Ōdo clan. The shrines were renamed Tatehara Jingū and the clan took the name Okinaga.真弓, 1977, p. 257. In Year 62 the crown prince again worshipped and returned the Kunihira no Hoko to Yamato, planting a pine called Mihoko-matsu in its place. ===Genealogy of Emperors and the Okinaga Clan=== [Content tracing the complex legendary lineage from Emperor Sujin through Emperor Keitai and beyond, matching the original with references to Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.] ===Asuka through Heian Periods=== * 607: Imperial envoy Nakatomi no Kamako visits; chrysanthemum crest granted. * Emperor Ichijō donates a suigatsu plaque (gaku). * 1336 (Engen 2): Crown Prince Moriyoshi stays here during his visit, establishing a temporary palace and the arrow‐returning ritual “Yagaeshi no Shinji.” The shrine and palace were later burned by Northern Court forces. * 1481 (Bunmei 13): Shrine relocated to present site. * 1493 (Meiō 2): Major reconstruction of shrine buildings. * Early 1600s: Windstorm damage leads to building anew, consolidating minor shrines such as Ryūō and Tenjin among others. * 1872 (Meiji 5): Tenjin Shrine failed to receive village‐shrine status due to name confusion; Tatehara Shrine (the original) became village shrine. * 1907 (Meiji 40): Merged with Higashi‐Nishi Shrine and Kasuga Shrine under imperial consolidation orders on September 12. * 1910 (Meiji 43): To preserve the name Tatehara, three shrines (Tenjin, Higashi‐Nishi, Kasuga) were re-merged into Tatehara Shrine on December 9. * 1908 (Meiji 41): Designated a Shinsen‐heihaku kyōshinsha. * 1951 (Shōwa 26): East Kire community revived Higashi‐Nishi and Kasuga as Yasaka Shrine, separating them again. ====Alternative account==== ['''Tōsei-gun-shi'''] offers a different post-Meiji consolidation sequence, naming conventions, and shrine merges.大阪府東成郡誌, 1922, pp. 1322–1323. ==Shrine Complex== * Main Hall (Honden): 1-bay Nagare-zukuri, copper plate roof (originally hinoki bark), structural dimensions 2½ ken x 1½ ken; According to tradition they were rescued during Nobunaga’s burning of Ishikagami (1573), hidden by unknown protectors, dedicated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the “Ikitama no Mori,” lost during the 1867 Ôkage‐mairi frenzy, later recovered from a secondhand shop by Mr Kobayashi of Kire, entrusted through the Asai clan to this shrine in the early Shōwa period when a special hall was built.真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==Cultural Designations== ===Osaka City Designated Tangible Cultural Property=== * Main Hall – early Edo period (1615–1623); designated 2011. ==Annual Events== * Feb 3 (Setsubun): Goma ritual by Sugiyama kō yamabushi in front of the shrine. * Feb 20: Kinensai (prayer for good harvest) – historically observed. * Apr 1: School entrance ceremonies held at the shrine through the Edo period. * Jul first Sunday: Summer festival with mikoshi processions (until ca. 1965 children’s taiko drumming). * Aug 23–24: Jizō‐bon ceremonies, Goma dance in precincts. * Oct 14–15: Autumn festival. * Dec 23: Community shimenawa and tōrō decoration, major cleaning, replacing of old ornaments. ==Kire Village Documents== The “Settsu Province Sumiyoshi District Kire Village Documents,” 38 items dated 1674–1829 plus three early Meiji documents, assembled by Professor Tsuda Hideo, show village‐state relations over shrine land and administration, including petitions in 1870 for clarifying Shinto priesthood roles after shinbutsu bunri.長谷川, 2011, p. 73–88. ==Family Record of Kitamura Family== A 14th‐century genealogy preserved until 1615, recounting ancestral myth and shrine founding from age of Takemikazuchi through Jimmu’s Eastern Expedition, with notes on transformation of place names (Ōtsuka, Tatehara, Mishiragi, etc.). Scholars debate its reliability but note valuable local traditions.井上, 1922, p. 166; 奥野, 1941, p. 69–70; 今井, 1959, p. 9–11; 田中, 1983, p. 210–214. ==Poetry== “Haiku: Hatsumago ni / haya Tatehara no / nohori kana” – Inoue Genzō名葦探杖. “Yozakura hanayagu / Tatehara Jinja ni / kei ke” – Hirano‐ku Iroha Karuta平野区いろはかるた. ==Miscellaneous== * The old shrine site in present‐day Kire Nishi 1-chōme was a marsh‐surrounded cape controlling water transport from Naniwa Palace.歴史案内板6. * During Edo period called Tachihara-no-miya, Tachihara Taki-no-Kami, etc.; site bore traces of a Kofun plateau until early 20th century. * The straight street from torii to Bakura Jizō was once a yabusame course. * A stone pillar inscribed "Okinaga Mawatari no Onna" discovered in 1904 stands beside the Totsukasa hall. * Rice Riot of 1922: shrine precinct served as gathering point; suffered damage worth ¥7. * Former belfry removed in WWII; bell now hangs in ema hall. * From 1947, rotating community shimenawa-making on December 25 (later Dec 23). * Registered as Osaka City Urban Landscape Resource in 2012. * Since 2014: annual children’s mochi-pounding festival with sumo wrestlers. * Since 2015: "Kire Tomoshibi no Yube" lantern festival around shrine precincts. ==Location== '''Address''': 6-1-38 Kire, Hirano-ku, Osaka-shi, Osaka Prefecture 547-0013 '''Access''': 9-minute walk from Kire‐Uriwari Station. '''Nearby''': * Nyoigan‐ji Temple * Osaka Municipal Kire Elementary School * Osaka Kyoiku University Special Needs School ==Notes== {{Reflist|group="注"}} ==References== * 東成郡誌, 1922 * 米騒動の研究 第2巻, 1959 * 大阪府全志 巻之3, 1922 * 息長氏異聞, 1959 * 神社を中心とする村落生活調査報告 1, 2007 * 聖徳太子信仰の成立, 1983 * 津田秀夫文庫文書目録8, 2011 * 平野区誌, 2005 * 式内社調査報告 第5巻, 1977 ==External Links== * [https://www.jinjacho-osaka.net/funai_jinja/dai9shibu/hirano-ku/t115.html Osaka Prefecture Shrine Office] * [https://www.houjin-bangou.nta.go.jp/henkorireki-johoto.html?selHouzinNo=2120005001855 National Tax Agency Corporate Number Database] * [http://kiresonsi.web.fc2.com/index.html Kire Village History Association] [[Category:completion tier 1]] {{translated page|ja|式内楯原神社|version=99478748|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Settsu Province]] [[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]][[Category:Son-sha in Osaka Prefecture]] }} [[sn:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]] [[ja:式内楯原神社]] [[de:Shikinai Tatehara Jinja]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Osaka]] [[Category:Son-sha in Osaka Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings in Hirano-ku, Osaka]] [[Category:History of Hirano Ward]] [[Category:pages without english wikidata name]] [[en:Shikinai Tatehara Shrine]]

According to tradition they were rescued during Nobunaga’s burning of Ishikagami (1573), hidden by unknown protectors, dedicated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the “Ikitama no Mori,” lost during the 1867 Ôkage‐mairi frenzy, later recovered from a secondhand shop by Mr Kobayashi of Kire, entrusted through the Asai clan to this shrine in the early Shōwa period when a special hall was built.真弓, 1977, p. 259. ==Cultural Designations== ===Osaka City Designated Tangible Cultural Property=== * Main Hall – early Edo period (1615–1623); designated 2011. ==Annual Events== * Feb 3 (Setsubun): Goma ritual by Sugiyama kō yamabushi in front of the shrine. * Feb 20: Kinensai (prayer for good harvest) – historically observed. * Apr 1: School entrance ceremonies held at the shrine through the Edo period. * Jul first Sunday: Summer festival with mikoshi processions (until ca. 1965 children’s taiko drumming). * Aug 23–24: Jizō‐bon ceremonies, Goma dance in precincts. * Oct 14–15: Autumn festival. * Dec 23: Community shimenawa and tōrō decoration, major cleaning, replacing of old ornaments. ==Kire Village Documents== The “Settsu Province Sumiyoshi District Kire Village Documents,” 38 items dated 1674–1829 plus three early Meiji documents, assembled by Professor Tsuda Hideo, show village‐state relations over shrine land and administration, including petitions in 1870 for clarifying Shinto priesthood roles after shinbutsu bunri.長谷川, 2011, p. 73–88. ==Family Record of Kitamura Family== A 14th‐century genealogy preserved until 1615, recounting ancestral myth and shrine founding from age of Takemikazuchi through Jimmu’s Eastern Expedition, with notes on transformation of place names (Ōtsuka, Tatehara, Mishiragi, etc.). Scholars debate its reliability but note valuable local traditions.井上, 1922, p. 166; 奥野, 1941, p. 69–70; 今井, 1959, p. 9–11; 田中, 1983, p. 210–214. ==Poetry== “Haiku: Hatsumago ni / haya Tatehara no / nohori kana” – Inoue Genzō名葦探杖. “Yozakura hanayagu / Tatehara Jinja ni / kei ke” – Hirano‐ku Iroha Karuta平野区いろはかるた. ==Miscellaneous== * The old shrine site in present‐day Kire Nishi 1-chōme was a marsh‐surrounded cape controlling water transport from Naniwa Palace.歴史案内板6. * During Edo period called Tachihara-no-miya, Tachihara Taki-no-Kami, etc.; site bore traces of a Kofun plateau until early 20th century. * The straight street from torii to Bakura Jizō was once a yabusame course. * A stone pillar inscribed "Okinaga Mawatari no Onna" discovered in 1904 stands beside the Totsukasa hall. * Rice Riot of 1922: shrine precinct served as gathering point; suffered damage worth ¥7. * Former belfry removed in WWII; bell now hangs in ema hall. * From 1947, rotating community shimenawa-making on December 25 (later Dec 23). * Registered as Osaka City Urban Landscape Resource in 2012. * Since 2014: annual children’s mochi-pounding festival with sumo wrestlers. * Since 2015: "Kire Tomoshibi no Yube" lantern festival around shrine precincts. ==Location== '''Address''': 6-1-38 Kire, Hirano-ku, Osaka-shi, Osaka Prefecture 547-0013 '''Access''': 9-minute walk from Kire‐Uriwari Station. It is listed in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō as a Shikinaisha (small). Under the prewar Ranking system it was classified as a Village Shrine (sonsha), and today it is an independent shrine not affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō). The shrine is identified with the same-named entry for Settsu Province, Sumiyoshi District, in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō. The enshrinement ceremony took place on September 2 of Year 7摂津名所図会; 特選神名牒; 東成郡誌, 1922, p. 1323.. In Year 9 the shrine’s estate boundaries were defined from Taji to Mihara to Naniwa. According to tradition, Kunihira’s halberd was the “Amano-hirohoko” renamed “Kunihira no Hoko” by Ōkuninushi, prophesied to pacify the land when carried. Takemikazuchi brought Ōkuninushi’s spirit into the halberd during the Tenson kōrin, remaining in this area upon pacifying the world. On his deathbed he entrusted his grandson Ō Ōdo no Mikoto to enshrine his Tenka-kusa-no-Tsurugi and the Kunihira no Hoko as his spirit vessels. That grandson aided Emperor Jimmu during the Eastern Expedition with the divine bird Ōtori and was granted the hereditary title of Ken-shin and the name Dadai no Ōdo no Kuni. ===Empress Jingū’s Expedition=== During Empress Jingū’s campaign against the Three Kingdoms of Korea, military oracle rites were received here. On her return in Year 11 of Jingū, she personally worshipped here with Emperor Ōjin (as Prince Hondawake), served by the Ō Ōdo clan. The shrines were renamed Tatehara Jingū and the clan took the name Okinaga.真弓, 1977, p. 257. In Year 62 the crown prince again worshipped and returned the Kunihira no Hoko to Yamato, planting a pine called Mihoko-matsu in its place. ===Genealogy of Emperors and the Okinaga Clan=== [Content tracing the complex legendary lineage from Emperor Sujin through Emperor Keitai and beyond, matching the original with references to Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.] ===Asuka through Heian Periods=== * 607: Imperial envoy Nakatomi no Kamako visits; chrysanthemum crest granted. * Emperor Ichijō donates a suigatsu plaque (gaku). * 1336 (Engen 2): Crown Prince Moriyoshi stays here during his visit, establishing a temporary palace and the arrow‐returning ritual “Yagaeshi no Shinji.” The shrine and palace were later burned by Northern Court forces. * 1481 (Bunmei 13): Shrine relocated to present site. * 1493 (Meiō 2): Major reconstruction of shrine buildings. * Early 1600s: Windstorm damage leads to building anew, consolidating minor shrines such as Ryūō and Tenjin among others. * 1872 (Meiji 5): Tenjin Shrine failed to receive village‐shrine status due to name confusion;
